description: Bionic Labs is building TerraTrace, an interactive Earth-system trend platform. It uses monthly NASA POWER records to explore how environmental variables change across locations and over time. Users select a variable and place, examine deseasonalised time series, and assess trends using the Mann–Kendall test, Sen’s slope and linear regression. We welcome collaborators in Earth science, climate research, statistics, GIS, data analysis, software development and science communication.
summary: TerraTrace is an interactive Earth-system trend investigation tool built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” It allows anyone to select a climate variable, choose a location on an interactive map, and analyse long-term monthly records from NASA POWER, extending from 1981 to the latest available data. TerraTrace transforms complex environmental time series into understandable evidence through interactive charts, seasonal-anomaly analysis, and statistical trend testing. It uses the Mann–Kendall test to assess trend significance, Sen’s slope to estimate the rate of change, and ordinary least squares to show the linear trend and fit quality. Users receive a plain-language verdict, can explore guided case studies, compare results, and export the underlying data as CSV. An optional AI briefing explains the already-computed statistics in accessible language. TerraTrace makes Earth-science data more approachable while clearly communicating uncertainty and the limitations of gridded data.
details:
TerraTrace turns the process of investigating environmental change into a guided, location-based experience. Instead of requiring users to manually download datasets, construct time series, write statistical scripts, and interpret technical results, the platform brings these steps together in one interactive workspace.

Github : https://github.com/Aaditya-Shah/terratrace

Users begin by selecting one of 13 monthly environmental variables available through NASA POWER, including air temperature, maximum and minimum temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind speed, dew point, solar radiation, surface soil wetness, root-zone soil wetness, and Earth skin temperature. They can search for a place, select a point on the interactive map, or launch one of 20 guided case studies covering locations such as the Amazon, the Sahel, the Arctic, and the Great Barrier Reef. They then choose a period of 20, 30, or 40 years, or investigate the full available record.

TerraTrace retrieves the corresponding NASA POWER monthly point data and performs the analysis using its own JavaScript statistical engine. For monthly series, it can remove the recurring seasonal cycle by comparing each month with its calendar-month average. It then applies the Mann–Kendall test to assess whether a consistent trend exists, Theil–Sen slope to estimate the robust rate of change, and ordinary least squares to calculate the linear fit and R². The results include the trend direction, rate per decade, total change, p-value, observations, and a visualised time series with a confidence band.

The platform also provides an interactive learning section explaining the variables and statistical methods, downloadable CSV data, and exportable PDF investigation reports. An optional OpenRouter-powered AI briefing translates the statistics already calculated by the platform into plain language. AI does not generate the underlying NASA measurements or determine the statistical result; the numerical analysis remains separate and reproducible.

The intended impact is to make long-term Earth-system evidence accessible to students, educators, researchers, and the wider public. TerraTrace encourages users to investigate how environmental conditions differ between locations, distinguish long-term signals from normal seasonal variation, and interpret statistical significance responsibly.

The project was developed using PHP, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, with MapLibre GL JS for interactive mapping, CARTO map styling, Photon geocoding, and jsPDF for PDF export. No specialised hardware is required.

Scientific limitations are made explicit: NASA POWER values are gridded estimates, not measurements from a sensor at the user's exact location. A statistically significant trend does not establish its cause, does not guarantee future conditions, and should not be treated as a forecast. TerraTrace is designed as an exploratory investigation and learning tool, not a substitute for local ground measurements or formal climate attribution.
